_comment: Day 5 evaluation set. 20 questions, written by hand.
WHY BY HAND. The task forbids LLM-generated questions, and the reason is
measurable rather than stylistic: a model writing a question from an
article reuses the article's own vocabulary, so the embedding of the
question lands next to the embedding of the passage almost by
construction. Retrieval then scores well because the question was drawn
from the answer, not because the search works. Every question below was
written after reading the article, deliberately in different words from
the source where possible.
THE TEN ARTICLES READ, and the ids they map to:
1  Some more things about Django I've been enjoying
2  Learning a few things about running SQLite
3  Moving away from Tailwind, and learning to structure my CSS
23  Some notes on starting to use Django
25  Notes on switching to Helix from vim
26  New zine: The Secret Rules of the Terminal
29  How to add a directory to your PATH
33  Why pipes sometimes get 'stuck': buffering
67  Cloudflare DDoS Threat Report H1 2026
111  Building better AI benchmarks: How many raters are enough?
COMPOSITION, as the task specifies: 7 single, 6 multi, 4 unanswerable,
3 vague.
ON must_contain FOR multi QUESTIONS. A `multi` question is one whose full
answer needs facts from two articles, so its must_contain holds a token
from each. That makes 'Answer correct' strictly harder than 'Top-1
correct' for these, which is the intended shape: a system that retrieves
one of the two articles and answers confidently from it alone should
lose the point.
ON must_contain STRINGS GENERALLY. They are matched case-insensitively
against the answer text. They are kept to the shortest token that is
genuinely load-bearing -- 'ANALYZE', '8KB' -- because a longer phrase
would test the model's phrasing rather than whether it found the fact.
Where a number or term can legitimately be written more than one way the
entry is a nested list of alternatives; see eval.py, which treats a
nested list as OR.

questions.question: Which command fixed the slow full-text search query, and how much faster did it get?
questions.note: DISAMBIGUATION: 7 articles mention SQLite. Only this one names ANALYZE.

questions.question: Why do the cleanup deletes cause a worker to crash?
questions.note: The chain is: a slow DELETE holds the write lock, another worker's 5s timeout expires, it crashes. Worded without 'timeout' or 'lock' on purpose.

questions.question: What are the two backup methods described for a SQLite database?
Why does adding a second grep to a pipe make the output disappear?
questions.note: Avoids the word 'buffering' so a match cannot come from the title alone.

questions.question: Which flag makes grep print each line immediately when writing to a pipe?
How do I tell which shell I am actually running?
If the wrong version of a program keeps running, what needs to change about PATH?
questions.note: The article says 'beginning'; 'front of your PATH' is equally correct and should not score wrong.

questions.question: Across both Django posts, what does the author like about migrations, and how many have they run?
questions.note: MULTI: 23 says migrations are generated automatically; only 1 gives the count of 19.

questions.question: What does the author use SQLite for in the Django project, and what problem did they hit operating it?
questions.note: MULTI: 23 explains choosing SQLite and backing up with VACUUM INTO; 2 holds the operational problem.

questions.question: How does the author describe Django's ORM syntax for joins, and what query builder pattern was built on top of it?
questions.note: MULTI: 23 introduces the `__` join syntax; 1 covers the EventQuerySet builder.

questions.question: What did the author keep from Tailwind after moving off it, and where else do they write about colour palettes?
questions.note: MULTI: 3 keeps the preflight reset; 4 is the separate colour-palettes links post it points at.

questions.question: What did the terminal zine cover, and which specific escape-code behaviour is documented separately?
questions.note: MULTI: 26 is the zine announcement, 28 is the ANSI-escape-codes deep dive. 'reset' was dropped from the second slot after checking article 28 -- it discusses `reset` nowhere (0 occurrences), so accepting it would have credited an answer the source cannot support. Ground truth is only ground truth if you grep for it.

questions.question: What editor did the author switch to, and what did they say about configuring their shell the same way?
questions.note: MULTI in intent: the fish comparison is what motivates the switch, and both halves live in 25, so the id list stays single. The type describes the question; eval.py scores against the ids either way.

questions.question: How many copies of the terminal zine were sold in the first week?
questions.note: NEAR-MISS: article 26 announces the zine and gives its $12 price, so the question lands squarely on a real article. Sales figures appear nowhere ('copies' does not occur in the article at all). REPLACED a first attempt -- 'what is the monthly hosting bill' -- which I wrote believing the corpus was silent on cost. It is not: article 1 says '~$10/month VM'. The system answered '$10 per month' and I had it marked as a hallucination. Grepping the corpus before trusting my own reading is the only thing that caught it.

questions.question: Which industry was the most attacked in the second half of 2026?
questions.note: NEAR-MISS: article 67 covers H1 2026 only and names Media, Production & Publishing as the #1 attacked industry for that half. H2 had not happened when the report was written. The question is answerable-looking and out of range, which is a different and more realistic failure than an absent topic. REPLACED 'which country launched the most DDoS attacks in H1 2026', which I asserted the report never covers -- it has a 'Top attack source countries' section naming Brazil at 14.9%. The system's answer was exactly right and my ground truth was wrong.

questions.question: What did it cost per rater to collect the DICES safety ratings?
questions.note: NEAR-MISS: article 111 names the DICES dataset with exact counts (350 conversations, 123 raters) and discusses annotation BUDGETS repeatedly, so the question sits on top of covered material. No per-rater cost is given anywhere. REPLACED 'how many raters does the paper recommend as a minimum', which I believed had no answer -- the article states plainly that practitioners 'often need more than 10 raters per item'. The system answered 'more than 10' and I had scored it a fabrication.

questions.question: What version of Helix fixed the panic in transaction.rs?
questions.note: NEAR-MISS: 25 quotes that exact panic and links the open issue. It never says it was fixed, in any version. Presupposition-loaded on purpose.

questions.question: sqlite analyze slow query django
questions.note: VAGUE: keywords, no grammar, no question mark. Same target as Q1; the pair measures what the lazy phrasing costs.

add folder to path zsh
